Do not plant the cuttings from the same stem, because they carry the virus. If you need clean cuttings, see ITRA or a registered producer.

history.content: My sorghum plants stay short and yellow even though the rains are good, what is happening?

draws.answer: Short, uniform plants with pale yellow leaves show nitrogen deficiency. First read the leaves; the pattern is yellowing that starts on the older lower leaves and climbs upward, without any streaks or spots, which points to nitrogen shortfall. Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK or a systemic fungicide because mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back on run-down soil. Bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Include a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, take a soil sample to ICAT for analysis and the proper dose for your plot.

history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: No, you cannot mix insecticides because they are not blended and one product does not become stronger by mixing. When you mix them you create a new product, not an enhanced one, and the strength is lost while the harm increases. There is no formula for making a stronger mix, and you do not get more control by mixing. The right thing to do is to use a product that is approved and correctly applied, and to ask ICAT which product is approved for the pest you are dealing with.

history.content: There is a strange purple weed around the base of my sorghum and the crop is not growing well. What steps do I take?

draws.answer: The weed is striga and you should first pull it out of the field before planting sorghum. Then sow sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing three to five grains per pocket at a depth of three to five centimetres and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Two to three weeks later thin the seedlings to two or three plants per pocket and carry out the first weeding without breaking the ridges. Apply NPK at 150 to 200 kilograms per hectare, followed by urea at 50 to 100 kilograms per hectare, and earth up to prevent lodging. When striga is present, plant a tolerant variety, for example TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, and ask ICAT for the suitable seed.

The weed is striga and it must be removed before sorghum flowers. Plant sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Two to three weeks after sowing, do the first weeding to keep the field tidy. Then pull any striga plants that show purple stems from the parent line. For the next season, choose a sorghum variety that tolerates striga, such as TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W. Consult ICAT to confirm striga and obtain a tolerant variety.

per_item.reference: It is not cassava brown streak disease, it is cassava mosaic disease because the leaf deformation is the key sign, not the root rot. First, pull up and destroy any plants that are strongly mottled and stunted. Then, for the next planting, collect cuttings only from plants that look healthy and avoid any mottled or deformed stems. After that, plant an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. Finally, do not move cuttings from fields that had the disease. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: My cassava plants have leaves that look pale and mottled and the leaves are twisted. I also see some brown, corky parts inside the roots after digging. Is this cassava brown streak disease?

draws.answer: Those signs indicate cassava brown streak disease caused by African cassava bacterial blight. First, use cuttings only from healthy plants because contaminated cuttings spread the disease. Then, remove and destroy the plants that show the pale leaves, twisted shape, and brown corky roots. Disinfect your tools between each plant to stop tool spread. After that, take cuttings only from plants that have even green leaves, normal shape, and no leaf distortion. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to a new site. For clean resistant cuttings you can contact ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the diagnosis.

It is cassava brown streak disease caused by African cassava mosaic disease. First, uproot and destroy the cassava plants that show cassava mosaic disease because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. Then, when you plant again, cut only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation, never from a mottled or twisted stem. Obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and plant them in a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: Striga hermonthica, known locally as witchweed, should be pulled by hand before it flowers and the uprooted plants burned to stop seed spread. After removal, add organic manure together with some urea and earth up the soil to weaken the weed and boost the sorghum. Finally, rotate or intercrop sorghum with a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For tolerant sorghum varieties or a multi-year rotation plan on a badly infested field, go to ICAT.

history.content: What management steps are recommended for Striga hermonthica on sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed that takes root in sorghum and pulls nitrogen away from the plant. First, pull out and destroy any plants that are strongly stunted, showing yellow or pale mottling and bunched, distorted young leaves. Then, for the next sowing, use a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level to keep the nodules in the soil. Also plant a tolerant sorghum variety and ask ICAT for a suitable improved variety.

Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed of sorghum, and the guidance is to use a sorghum variety that tolerates or is resistant to it, to pull the Striga plants out before they flower, and to avoid sowing sorghum on the same plot two years in a row. Do not grow sorghum on the same field more than two years consecutively. For variety selection, visit ICAT, and you can ask about resistant varieties.

history.content: why sorghum stays stunted yellow

draws.answer: The yellowing is caused by nitrogen shortage after long rains, not a disease. First, read the leaves: uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves shows the plant is hungry for nitrogen, not that a fungus is present. Second, do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's recommendation because mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back on depleted soil. Third, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, take a soil sample to ICAT for analysis and the correct dose for your plot.

Stunting caused by sorghum is a nitrogen shortage on depleted soil. First, look for uniform pale yellowing of older leaves as the symptom, not a spot or a dead-heart. Second, do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word because mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back on run-down soil. Third, bring organic matter back by applying manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot before any large purchase. ICAT is the service to consult.

history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: No, you cannot mix insecticides because they are not blended and one product does not become stronger by mixing. An insecticide is a product that controls insects, and mixing two or more of them changes the behavior of the chemicals. When you mix them you create a new product, not an enhanced one, and the strength is lost while the harm increases. There is no formula for making a stronger mix, and you do not get more control by mixing. The right thing to do is to use a product that is approved and correctly applied, and to ask ICAT which product is approved for the pest you are dealing with.

No, you must never mix an insecticide with a vaporizer together, as the product names on the container tell you not to do that and the label says that. The label is written in English, and the label is the part that can be read by another person. What the label says is the order: read the product and its rate before you add any diluent, and never make the mix darker than the product. The mixture does not make the product stronger, it makes it more dangerous for you, for children and for animals. If the label says to use the rate without the product name, that name is on the container anyway, so read it too.

history.content: My goats have a mucky discharge from their eyes and some are dying quickly. What steps must I take?

draws.answer: This is a tick-borne disease, so call the veterinary service the same day and tell them the urine colour; red to black indicates redwater, yellow-brown without red indicates gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on every animal. Never reuse a needle between animals. The veterinary service will identify the exact disease and provide the correct drug and dose. You must see the veterinary service the same day.

Mucky discharge in the eyes is a sign of leucaena poisoning. Cut leucaena back so it is only a quarter to a third of the ration and never the main feed. Mix the remaining leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen enough roughage. Introduce the new mix gradually over several days. Ensure the goats always have clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the animals keep losing appetite or drool, see the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: Your goats are suffering from peste des petits ruminants (PPR). Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My goats have fever and a thick discharge from their noses and eyes.
Do you also see sores inside the mouth or coughing in the affected animals?
Yes, they have sores in the mouth and some are coughing.

draws.answer: Your goats are suffering from a tick-borne disease such as gall sickness caused by Anaplasma marginale or redwater caused by Babesia bigemina or Babesia bovis. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify the parasite and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine you observed, red to black means redwater, yellow-brown without red means gall sickness. Keep the sick goats in the shade, give them clean water and do not let them walk because they lack red blood cells. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick goat, to stop further spread. Never use the same needle on two animals because gall sickness travels on a contaminated needle. You should see the veterinary service the same day.

The problem is called leucaena poisoning, which occurs when leucaena makes up too much of the ration. Cut the leucaena back so it is only a quarter to a third of the total feed and never the main component. Mix the reduced leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen plenty of roughage. Introduce the feed mix gradually over several days and always keep clean water and a mineral or salt source available. If the gums, eyelids or bellies stay swollen, see the veterinary service.

Hand-pick all ticks you see on every animal in the herd. Never use the same needle on two different goats. The veterinary service is the only one you should see for diagnosis and treatment.

Always provide clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the condition does not improve, see the veterinary service.

history.content: My neighbor says his cassava looks fine, but I see some brown spots inside the roots when I pull them up. Can I take cuttings from his field?

First, walk the plot and pull every cassava plant showing angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves, shoot die-back or gum on stem. Inhale the air and observe the leaves to confirm the disease. Remove and destroy all affected plants to stop the bacterium from moving. Disinfect your tools between each plant you handle. Use cuttings only from plants that show no signs of disease. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the diagnosis.

Then plant those cuttings in a single row, planting two to three plants per pocket with each pocket one metre by one metre. Place the cassava two to three metres from the edge of the plot. Weed the cassava two to three times while the plants are still small. For clean improved cuttings you should contact ITRA or a registered producer.

history.content: I see a purple flowered weed around the base of my short sorghum plants, what should I do?

draws.answer: The purple-flowered Striga is a parasitic plant that will take over the root system of your sorghum. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting 4-5 grains per pocket at 3-5 cm depth and using 6-8 kg per hectare of treated seed. When the seedlings are 3-4 weeks old, carry out the first weeding without breaking the ridges. Then plant a cereal after the sorghum in the same field. Between sorghum and the cereal, use a legume such as cowpea or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. For seed that is resistant to Striga, consult ICAT.

The purple-flowered Striga is a parasitic weed that needs to be removed before short sorghum can grow. Look into the ground and pull out any Striga plants that are growing in the field. Then, when you return to the sorghum, sow a line of groundnut or cowpea in the same spot and keep the rows 80 cm apart. Keep the sorghum rows 40 cm apart from each groundnut or cowpea row and plant the sorghum 2-3 seeds per pocket at 3-5 cm depth. Wait two weeks after the sorghum was planted to sow the groundnut or cowpea. For any questions about the sorghum variety, see ICAT.

history.content: how far should fields be spaced to avoid spread

draws.answer: The spacing depends on which variety you plant in a rotation, and both TZEE W Pop STR QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W are 90 to 100 days and ACR97 L Sotubaka 75 to 85 days, so use the cycle length for the spacing. If you put a legume in the rotation, widen the spacing between the legume plants. One spacing rule is to avoid growing maize on the same plot two years in a row, because it reduces parasite pressure. For a rotation suited to your plot, see ICAT.

Spacing is the practice you can control. For maize with a grain, 80 to 100 days: 3 to 4 cm between rows and 15 to 20 cm between pockets. For maize with beans or cowpea: 40 to 50 days, 3 to 4 cm between rows and 20 to 25 cm between pockets, or 20 to 25 days, 2 to 3 cm between rows and 20 to 25 cm between pockets. If you grow with a legume such as cowpea or groundnut, widen the spacing by 10 to 20 cm. Sow the seed in June and July for two crops in the same year.

history.content: What steps should I take to manage Striga hermonthica in my sorghum crop?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed that takes root in sorghum and cuts the water and nutrients the plant needs. Plant a sorghum variety that is tolerant to Striga. Before sowing, read the leaf pattern: a uniform pale yellow on older lower leaves means the weed is Striga. Do not use the same seed next season; pull the striga plants out before they flower. If you need help choosing a tolerant variety, go to ICAT.

Striga is the weed that grows in the same soil as your sorghum and starves the plant of nutrients. To control it, sow a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field right after the sorghum and cut the legume stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Then weed early, doing the first weeding about two weeks after sowing the sorghum. If you later see Striga plants, go to ICAT for help.

draws.answer: The problem is leucaena poisoning caused by leucaena being made the main feed. Cut the leucaena back so it makes only about a quarter to a third of the ration and never let it dominate the diet. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen gets plenty of roughage. Introduce this new mix gradually over a few days, and always provide constant clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the goats keep refusing to eat, keep drooling, or develop a swollen throat, see the veterinary service.

This is leucaena poisoning from a sudden shift to leucaena in a short time. Cut leucaena back to a supplement, roughly a quarter to a third of the ration, and never let it be the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen has plenty of roughage. Change the feed composition gradually over several days. Ensure the animals always have clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the signs do not improve, contact the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: These observations match PPR, peste des petits ruminants, a fast and highly contagious virus that hits goats hard. You must isolate every sick goat immediately and stop all movement of animals into or out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any goats for market while the disease is present, and make sure any carcasses are disposed of safely. Provide water and soft feed to the sick goats to support them. Then vaccinate all healthy and in-contact goats with the PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: My goats are dying fast, they have fever, runny eyes and noses, and some have mouth sores, what is the problem?

draws.answer: I will not name a disease from those signs, because two of my four tests give false positive results. Fever and eye or nose discharge are symptoms of many diseases, and a sore mouth is not something the veterinary service can see at a glance. Call the veterinary service today, and let them look at the animals. While you wait, separate the sick ones from the healthy ones, do not make them walk, and keep water in the shade with clean drinkers. Do not eat grass until they have been seen.

Those signs are typical of a tick-borne disease: gall sickness, also called redwater, spread by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify if it is gall sickness or redwater and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, red to black points to redwater and yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick goats in the shade, give clean water and do not make them walk. Hand-pick all ticks you see on every animal in the herd, not just the sick one. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service will provide the proper treatment.

history.content: My sheep are coughing, have diarrhoea and some are dying fast, what should I do?

draws.answer: Those signs point to a tick-borne disease such as gall sickness or redwater. Call the veterinary service the same day and tell them the urine colour; red to black indicates redwater, yellow-brown without red indicates gall sickness. Keep the sick sheep in the shade, give it clean water, and avoid making it walk. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick one. The veterinary service will diagnose the exact disease and give the correct drug and dose.

per_item.reference: Those are signs of cassava brown streak disease on cassava. First, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy and plant a variety that tolerates the disease. Next, pull out any cassava plants showing the yellow leaf veins or the brown corky rot in the roots and destroy them completely. Also, avoid moving any cuttings from fields where those symptoms appear. history.content: My cassava leaves have yellow streaks on the veins and when I dig up the roots they are brown and corky. What should I do?

draws.answer: Those signs are cassava bacterial blight. Pull out each plant with the yellow or pale streaks along the veins and the brown, corky rot in the roots and destroy them. Clean your tools with a disinfectant before you work on the next plant. Only take cuttings from plants that have even green leaves and no damage. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to a new site. If you need clean cuttings, go to ITRA or a registered producer.

Those signs indicate bacterial blight, so you must remove and destroy all affected plants right away. After removal, disinfect your cutting tools between each plant you handle. Choose only plants that have no yellow streaks, no corky lesions, and no wilting leaves. Plant a resistant cassava variety in the cleared area and rotate the plot for the next season. Get clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer and ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.

per_item.reference: Striga, known locally as witchweed, can be managed by first feeding the soil with organic manure and a small amount of urea; this weakens the parasite and boosts sorghum health. Then pull the witchweed by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted plants to prevent seed spread. Follow with a rotation or intercrop using a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For severe infestations, see ICAT for tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the weed that competes with sorghum for water and nutrients. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five grains per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Two weeks after sowing, do the first weeding to keep the field clear of weeds. Then plant a sorghum tolerant variety if you expect Striga to occur. For seed of a resistant variety, contact ICAT.

Striga is the weed that attaches to sorghum and limits the root system, so pull it out before the plants reach two to three months old. Then sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five grains per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Two to three weeks after sowing thin the seedlings to two to three metres apart. Keep the first weeding about two weeks after sowing and do the three flowering-stage sprays for pod protection. For seed, visit ICAT for a tolerant variety.
